title: The Naturalist
subtitle: Roosevelt and the Natural World
intro: He founded a museum in his bedroom at nine, learned taxidermy from a man who had travelled with Audubon, and grew into a president who could correct professional ornithologists over dinner. Fifteen questions on the science that ran underneath everything else he did.

tiers.name: First Specimen
tiers.line: His was a seal skull. Start somewhere.

questions.prompt: What did the young Roosevelt call his boyhood collection?
options: The Roosevelt Museum of Natural History
questions.explanation: The Roosevelt Museum of Natural History, founded with two cousins and equipped with its own labels. It spread out of his bedroom and through the house, to the visible strain of the household staff.
questions.credit: The Roosevelt children. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

link.label: Building a museum in his bedroom

questions.prompt: What was the museum's first specimen?
options: A robin's egg taken in Central Park
questions.explanation: He came across a dead seal laid out on a plank in a market on Broadway, went back day after day to measure it, and eventually got hold of the head so that he could clean the skull. That skull became the first item in the collection, and he traced his whole interest in natural history back to that one animal — a boy with a folding rule, taking the measurements of something he had only ever read about.
questions.credit: The Roosevelt children. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Who taught him taxidermy, and what was that man's claim to fame?
options: John G. Bell, who travelled with Audubon
Carl Akeley, who pioneered the museum diorama
questions.explanation: John G. Bell kept a musty little taxidermy shop on Broadway and had gone west with John James Audubon. Roosevelt took lessons there as a boy and mounted his own specimens for years afterwards. Bell is also the reason the collection stopped being a heap — a seal skull here, a turtle shell there, some mice caught in the pantry — and started being something with labels and a method behind it.
questions.imageAlt: The Roosevelt children and companions in Dresden
questions.credit: Dresden Literary American Club. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt intend to become when he entered Harvard in 1876?
questions.explanation: He went up meaning to be a scientist — a field naturalist of the kind Bell and Audubon had been. What put him off was the direction the discipline was taking: Harvard science by the 1870s meant the laboratory and the microscope rather than the outdoor field study he loved. He turned to history and politics instead, and never stopped doing natural history on the side.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt as a college student
questions.credit: "Theo. Roosevelt at college." Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Which institution did Roosevelt's father help found?
options: The American Museum of Natural History
questions.explanation: Theodore Roosevelt Sr. was among the founders of the American Museum of Natural History in New York — an institution that his son supplied with specimens as a boy and supported all his life.
questions.imageAlt: The Fraser equestrian statue in front of the Roosevelt Memorial, New York City
questions.credit: Fraser statue of T.R. in front of Roosevelt Memorial, New York City. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt published his first natural history work at what stage of life?
options: He never published on natural history
questions.explanation: He was eighteen, with one year of college behind him. The Summer Birds of the Adirondacks in Franklin County, N.Y. appeared in 1877 — a four-page catalogue written in the mountains with a Harvard friend, Henry Davis Minot, and printed at their own expense. Roosevelt had gone up to Harvard the previous autumn, so it is an undergraduate's pamphlet, and it made him a published naturalist four years before he was a published historian.
questions.imageAlt: Holworthy Hall in Harvard Yard, photographed in the nineteenth century
questions.credit: Holworthy Hall, Harvard Yard. Photograph by William Notman & Son. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What was the primary stated purpose of Roosevelt's 1909 African expedition?
questions.explanation: Scientific collecting, and the expedition sent home many thousands of specimens. Roosevelt was quite clear that the shooting served the collecting. The scale of it has drawn criticism ever since, and he defended it as museum work.
questions.imageAlt: Measuring a rhinoceros horn on the African expedition
questions.credit: Putting the tape on the rhino's horn. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Which naturalist and museum taxidermist appears alongside Roosevelt in African expedition photographs?
questions.explanation: Carl Akeley, the pioneer of the museum habitat diorama, whose work transformed how the public saw wildlife. His methods are why natural history museums look the way they do.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt, Carl Akeley and an elephant
questions.credit: Father, Akeley, and elephant. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt publicly attacked a group of popular writers in 1907. What was his objection?
options: They lifted passages from his books
They opposed the creation of forest reserves
questions.explanation: The “nature fakers” controversy. Roosevelt, backed by John Burroughs, went after authors whose animal stories attributed impossible reasoning and behaviour to wild creatures. He thought sentimental invention passed off as observation did real damage to how people understood nature. The offender he named most often was the Reverend William J. Long, and the row played out in the magazines through 1907 with a sitting president as one of the combatants.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt reading in front of his tent at Kijabe
questions.credit: Roosevelt reading in front of his tent in camp at Kijabe. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt famously do at Pelican Island, Florida, in 1903?
options: Established the first federal bird reservation
questions.explanation: He made it the first federal bird reservation, to stop plume hunters destroying the colony for the hat trade. Fifty more reservations followed — the beginnings of the national wildlife refuge system.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt and Pinchot on the Mississippi with the Inland Waterways Commission
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt and Gifford Pinchot on the Mississippi River, Inland Waterways Commission. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. One frame of a stereograph card; publisher's mount and negative number cropped away.

questions.prompt: How good was Roosevelt's practical field knowledge of birds?
options: He had largely lost interest by adulthood
Good enough to identify birds by song
Limited to the North American species he hunted
Superficial — he leaned on professional guides
questions.explanation: He identified birds by ear, kept lists everywhere he went, and on a walk through the English countryside in 1910 with the British statesman Edward Grey he named the species by song as they went. Grey, himself a serious birdwatcher, was impressed. He was also willing to argue the point with professional ornithologists, in print, while holding federal office.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt reading in front of his tent
questions.credit: Roosevelt reading in front of his tent in hunting camp. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. Cropped from the album mount.

questions.prompt: Which of Roosevelt's books came out of his Dakota years as a working naturalist and hunter?
questions.explanation: Hunting Trips of a Ranchman, published in 1885 and illustrated in part by Frederic Remington. It was followed by Ranch Life and the Hunting-Trail and later The Wilderness Hunter — all part natural history, part memoir.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt in buckskin with a rifle, 1885
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt in 1885. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt see in the Dakota Badlands that shaped his view of wildlife forever?
options: The first grizzly bears he had seen
questions.explanation: He arrived in 1883 just months after commercial hunters had destroyed the last great herd on the Little Missouri. He hunted the survivors and wrote about the bones scattered across the prairie. It is the single clearest source of his later conviction that unrestricted use was theft from the future.
questions.credit: Cattle on the range. Photograph by L. A. Huffman. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University. Publisher's mount and caption strip removed.

questions.prompt: Which conservation and hunting organisation did Roosevelt co-found in 1887?
questions.explanation: The Boone and Crockett Club, founded with George Bird Grinnell to campaign for game laws and the protection of Yellowstone. Its members were hunters, and their argument was that without protection there would be nothing left to hunt.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt and John Muir in Yosemite
questions.credit: Yosemite, Cal., with John Muir. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How did Roosevelt describe the relationship between his hunting and his science?
options: He regarded hunting as purely recreational
He kept the two entirely separate
He abandoned science when he began hunting
questions.explanation: He saw no contradiction: specimens had to be collected before they could be studied, and field observation mattered more to him than laboratory work. Collecting and observation were the point and the rifle was the means — that is how he described it and how he defended it. Modern readers often find it hard to reconcile, and it is a fair tension to sit with rather than explain away.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt reading at camp in Kijabe
questions.credit: Roosevelt reading in front of his tent in camp at Kijabe. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.
